gloss_distractors: to put in the right order
senses.definition: To keep something from being seen or understood, often without meaning to.
senses.caution: It blames nobody, unlike obfuscate, which says someone meant to mislead. Use it about things such as charts, since about a person's explanation it is still a criticism.
senses.example: The monthly average obscures the two days when latency tripled, so let us show the daily line instead.

cues.text: A monthly rollup is hiding the two bad days inside it, and you want a neutral word for what the rollup is doing.
A summary metric is correct but stops people seeing the variance underneath, and you want to say so without implying anyone did it on purpose.
Fog has taken the mountains at the end of the valley out of view, and you want a slightly formal word for what it is doing.

distractors: To show a result in a chart so that the trend is easy to see.
To say something more plainly than it was said the first time.
To put a set of numbers in order so the largest ones come first on the page.
To remove a detail from a report because it was found to be wrong after checking.
To repeat a point until everyone in the room has heard it at least once.

senses.definition: Little known, so that most people have never heard of it.
senses.caution: Saying something is obscure can sound like showing off. Say who does know it, for example only the data team, so it does not read as a put-down.
senses.example: It is an obscure setting in the load balancer, and I doubt anyone outside the platform team knows it exists.

cues.text: You are pushing back on a reference to a library that almost nobody in the room will have heard of.
A candidate's CV lists a certification you have never seen, and you ask a colleague whether anyone recognises it.
A friend recommends a film that almost nobody has seen, and you want a word for how little known it is.

distractors: Known to almost everyone in the field.
Out of date, and replaced by something newer.
Used by many teams but owned by nobody in particular.
Written so clearly that anyone can follow it the first time.
Expensive to run, and so kept only for the most important work.
